title: Metadata Exposure Review
objective: Run the post-incident review of a link-preview web app whose EC2 role credentials were used from an unexpected IP: find the exposure path, contain it (revoke sessions, harden the metadata service), and rebuild the role to least privilege.
successCriteria: You identified why a server-side URL fetch can reach the instance metadata service, and which instance settings made it worse
You spotted the role session used from an IP that is not the instance, and contained it by revoking older sessions and enforcing IMDSv2 with hop limit 1
You rewrote the instance role policy so it can touch only the app's own bucket prefix and table
hints: Start with the evidence: instance settings (describe-instances), the role attached to the instance profile, and what CloudTrail says that role's session did and from where.

Containment has two halves: invalidate credentials that were already issued, and make sure the instance cannot hand out credentials the same way again. Compare MetadataOptions in the artifact with what you want them to be.

Use aws iam put-role-policy with a deny-before-timestamp document on LinkPreviewRole (see revoke-older-sessions.json), then aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options with --http-tokens required and --http-put-response-hop-limit 1. Re-run describe-instances to verify.

range.scenario: ShopCo's security team got a GuardDuty finding: credentials belonging to the instance role of `link-preview` (a web app on EC2 that fetches any URL a user pastes and returns a page snippet) were used from an IP address that is not the instance. You are the incident responder in account 111122223333 with the `IncidentResponderRole` (read access plus the ability to modify IAM and EC2 metadata settings). Review the evidence, work out how the credentials could leave the instance, contain the incident, and fix the root causes so it cannot recur. Everything is simulated; use the terminal like the AWS CLI.

tasks.prompt: Read preview_service.py. Why can a feature that fetches a user-supplied URL end up exposing the instance's role credentials?
options: The fetch is made by the instance itself, so the link-local metadata address that only the instance can reach is reachable too; the app acts as a proxy into it and returns whatever answers
The metadata service has a public IP address, so any visitor can reach it directly once the app is running
Flask exposes environment variables in every JSON response by default
The instance security group allows inbound traffic on port 80, which is what the metadata service listens on
tasks.explanation: The metadata service lives on a link-local address that is only routable from the instance's own network stack. A server-side request made on a user's behalf runs from that stack, so the application becomes a confused deputy that can be steered at internal-only endpoints. The code never validates the destination, the scheme or the redirect target, which is the classic server-side request forgery weakness.

tasks.prompt: Review the CloudTrail evidence. Which source IP address used the role session from somewhere other than the instance's public IP (203.0.113.10)?
tasks.explanation: Instance-role credentials are meant to be used from the instance. A session that suddenly appears from a different public IP, with a different user agent, listing buckets and then reading a customer export, is the signature of credentials that left the instance. The IP and user agent are your pivot points for scoping what was accessed.

tasks.prompt: Which settings in instance-metadata-options.json made this exposure easier? Select all that apply.
options: HttpTokens: optional, so IMDSv1 style plain GET requests are accepted without a session token
HttpPutResponseHopLimit: 2, so a token response can travel one extra network hop, for example through a forwarding layer or container
InstanceMetadataTags: disabled
State: applied
tasks.explanation: With HttpTokens optional, any request that can issue a simple GET is enough to read credentials. IMDSv2 requires a PUT to obtain a session token first and a token header on later reads, which a forwarded GET-only request usually cannot supply. A hop limit of 1 also stops the token response from being forwarded beyond the instance. Disabled instance tags and the applied state are not risk factors.

tasks.prompt: Contain the incident from the terminal: invalidate the role sessions that were already issued, enforce IMDSv2 with hop limit 1 on the instance, and then verify the instance. Paste the flag the security-ops verification tag shows.
tasks.explanation: Containment needs both halves. Revoking older sessions kills the stolen credentials that still have hours left to live; hardening the metadata service stops the instance from issuing credentials to the same kind of request again. Doing only one leaves either live stolen credentials or a reusable exposure path.

tasks.prompt: When you use the IAM console's 'Revoke active sessions' on a role, it attaches an inline deny policy to the role. What is that policy conventionally named?
tasks.explanation: AWSRevokeOlderSessions denies all actions where aws:TokenIssueTime is earlier than the time you revoke. It does not delete credentials; it makes older sessions useless while new sessions, issued after the cutoff, keep working. Remember to also rotate any long-lived secrets the role could read, because the attacker may have copied them.

tasks.prompt: Rebuild the instance role policy to least privilege. The app must read and write thumbnails under s3://shopco-link-previews and read, write and query the DynamoDB table LinkPreviewCache in us-east-1. It must not list buckets, read other buckets, read secrets, or delete tables.

tests.name: App can write thumbnails to its bucket
App can read thumbnails from its bucket
App cannot read the customer exports bucket
App cannot delete its own table

tasks.explanation: The stolen session could read the customer exports bucket only because the role had s3:* on every resource. Least privilege means naming the exact actions and ARNs the workload uses, so a credential leak exposes only what the app already needed. Blast radius is the part of an incident you control in advance.

tasks.prompt: Which application-level fix best removes the root cause in preview_service.py?
options: Only fetch hostnames from an approved allow-list, restrict schemes to https, resolve the name and reject loopback, private and link-local addresses on the resolved IP, and do not follow redirects blindly
Reject URLs that contain the literal text of the metadata IP address
Check that the URL starts with https:// and nothing else
Increase the request timeout so that internal requests fail more often
tasks.explanation: A string deny-list is easy to sidestep because the same destination can be written in other forms or reached through a hostname that resolves to it or a redirect. Validate the destination after resolution, prefer an allow-list, and treat redirects as new requests that need the same checks. Keep IMDSv2 and least privilege as defence in depth: application bugs will happen, so the platform should limit the damage.

takeaways: Server-side fetch features can reach internal-only endpoints such as the metadata service; validate destinations after DNS resolution, allow-list where possible, and do not follow redirects blindly.
Contain credential exposure in two moves: revoke already-issued sessions (deny before a timestamp) and close the path that issued them (IMDSv2 required, hop limit 1).
Give instance roles only the actions and ARNs the workload needs; the role's permissions define the blast radius when its credentials leak.

title: Enforce IMDSv2
objective: Audit a fleet of EC2 instances for IMDSv2 compliance, harden every non-compliant instance with HttpTokens=required and hop limit 1, verify the result, and write an SCP that stops new non-compliant launches.
successCriteria: You found every instance that does not meet the standard (HttpTokens required and hop limit 1) and hardened them
You verified the fleet with a describe and a compliance check, and checked for IMDSv1 callers before enforcing
You wrote an SCP that denies launching instances without IMDSv2 and with a hop limit above 1
hints: The standard has two parts: HttpTokens and the hop limit. An instance can fail on either one, so look at both columns.
describe-instances shows MetadataOptions for the whole fleet. Fix each non-compliant instance with modify-instance-metadata-options, then re-check.

For an instance that is already 'required' but has hop limit 2, only the hop limit needs lowering. For the SCP, use a Deny on ec2:RunInstances with the ec2:MetadataHttpTokens condition key (StringNotEquals required) and a NumericGreaterThan on ec2:MetadataHttpPutResponseHopLimit.

resources.title: AWS docs: Configure the instance metadata service
AWS Security Blog: Defense in depth against SSRF and the EC2 metadata service

range.scenario: After an SSRF incident, Security Engineering published a standard: every EC2 instance in account 111122223333 must require IMDSv2 and use a metadata hop limit of 1. You have been handed the `SecurityAuditRole` and five instances in us-east-1 to check, fix and sign off. Some already comply, some do not in different ways, and one of them runs a legacy workload nobody wants to break. Work out which instances are non-compliant, harden them with the simulated AWS CLI, confirm the fleet is clean, and then close the door for future launches with a service control policy.

artifacts.name: imds-standard.txt
artifacts.content:
Instance Metadata Service standard (Security Engineering, v3)

1. HttpTokens must be 'required' (IMDSv2 only). No IMDSv1 exceptions.
2. HttpPutResponseHopLimit must be 1 unless a documented exception exists (none are on file).
3. HttpEndpoint stays 'enabled' (workloads need role credentials).
4. New launches must be blocked at the Organizations level if they do not set (1) and (2).
5. Before enforcing on a running instance, confirm via CloudWatch metric MetadataNoToken that nothing still calls IMDSv1.
artifacts.note: The compliance standard you are auditing against.

artifacts.name: launch-template-app-base.json
artifacts.note: The launch template used to build most of the fleet. It explains how non-compliant instances keep appearing.

artifacts.name: current-scp.json
artifacts.note: The SCP currently attached to the workloads OU: it allows everything.

terminal.intro: Assumed SecurityAuditRole in account 111122223333. Region: us-east-1. Fleet: 5 instances.
terminal.help:
Commands you can try (like the AWS CLI):
  aws sts get-caller-identity
  aws ec2 describe-instances
  aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id <id> --http-tokens required --http-put-response-hop-limit 1
  aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name MetadataNoToken --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=<id> --statistics Sum --period 3600 --start-time 2026-11-19T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-11-20T00:00:00Z
  aws configservice get-compliance-details-by-config-rule --config-rule-name imds-hardening-check

usage: aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id <id> [--http-tokens optional|required] [--http-put-response-hop-limit <n>] [--http-endpoint enabled|disabled]
error: --instance-id is required

tasks.prompt: Why do HttpTokens=required and HttpPutResponseHopLimit=1 together make it much harder to read role credentials through a server-side request forgery bug?
options: IMDSv2 needs a session token obtained with a PUT request and sent in a header on later reads, which a simple forwarded GET cannot supply, and hop limit 1 keeps the token response from being forwarded off the instance
IMDSv2 encrypts the role credentials with a key stored on the instance, so intercepted traffic is unreadable
Hop limit 1 blocks all outbound traffic from the instance
IMDSv2 moves the metadata service to a public endpoint protected by the instance security group
tasks.explanation: IMDSv2 is session-oriented: the caller must first request a short-lived token with a PUT, then present it on every metadata read. Typical SSRF bugs only let an attacker issue a plain GET, and the hop limit keeps token responses from crossing a forwarding hop. It is a mitigation that raises the bar, not a substitute for fixing the application bug.

tasks.prompt: Use describe-instances. How many of the five instances do NOT meet the standard (HttpTokens required and hop limit 1)? Reply with a number.
tasks.explanation: Two instances pass; three fail in different ways: one allows IMDSv1 and has hop limit 2, one allows IMDSv1 with hop limit 1, and one requires tokens but has hop limit 2. An audit that only checks HttpTokens misses the last one, so check every control in the standard.

tasks.prompt: Harden every non-compliant instance, then run the AWS Config compliance check for imds-hardening-check. When the whole fleet is compliant, paste the flag in the attestation annotation.
tasks.explanation: Each instance needed a different change: two needed IMDSv2 enforced, and two needed the hop limit lowered. Verifying with a compliance rule rather than assuming success is what makes the audit defensible, and re-running it periodically catches drift when new instances launch from an old template.

tasks.prompt: Before enforcing HttpTokens=required on a running production instance, which signal tells you whether something is still calling the metadata service the old IMDSv1 way and would break?
options: The CloudWatch metric MetadataNoToken for that instance (metadata calls made without a session token)
The CPUUtilization metric for that instance
The StatusCheckFailed metric for that instance
The NetworkIn metric for the instance's network interface
tasks.explanation: MetadataNoToken counts metadata requests that did not use a token, in other words IMDSv1 calls. If it is non-zero, something on the instance (often an old SDK or agent) will lose access to credentials after enforcement, so upgrade it first or schedule the change. A zero count lets you enforce with confidence.

tasks.prompt: Query MetadataNoToken for the instances you plan to enforce. Which instance name still has callers using IMDSv1?
tasks.explanation: legacy-reports is still making token-less calls, so enforcing IMDSv2 will break whatever software is doing that until its SDK or agent is updated to use IMDSv2. The right response is to fix the caller and then enforce, not to leave the instance on IMDSv1 forever. Coordinate with the owner, set a deadline, and track it as an exception until it closes.

tasks.prompt: What is the IAM condition key, used in an SCP or IAM policy for ec2:RunInstances, that carries the HttpTokens value requested for the new instance?
tasks.explanation: ec2:MetadataHttpTokens lets you write a policy such as 'deny RunInstances unless the value is required'. A companion key, ec2:MetadataHttpPutResponseHopLimit, lets you cap the hop limit. Policies that prevent a bad configuration at creation time scale better than auditing after the fact.

tasks.prompt: Write the guardrail for current-scp.json: keep the allow-all statement, and add denies so that ec2:RunInstances on instance resources is refused unless HttpTokens is 'required', and refused when the hop limit is greater than 1.

tests.name: Launch with IMDSv2 required and hop limit 1 is allowed
Launch that leaves IMDSv1 enabled is denied
Launch with IMDSv2 required but hop limit 2 is denied
Launch that states no HttpTokens value at all is denied

tasks.explanation: A Deny with StringNotEquals on ec2:MetadataHttpTokens refuses anything except 'required', and because a negated operator is true when the key is missing, a launch that omits the setting is blocked too. The hop-limit statement uses NumericGreaterThan so values above 1 are refused. SCPs never grant, which is why the allow-all statement stays: the SCP only fences what identity policies can grant.

takeaways: A compliance standard has several parts: check each control (HttpTokens and hop limit), not just the headline one.
Check MetadataNoToken before enforcing IMDSv2 on running instances, and fix legacy callers rather than leaving exceptions open.
Detect drift with AWS Config and prevent it at creation time with an SCP using ec2:MetadataHttpTokens, and fix the launch templates that keep producing non-compliant instances.

title: Expose Audit
objective: Audit security groups for ports reachable from 0.0.0.0/0, list the findings through the simulated CLI, remediate each to least privilege (revoke the open rule, add a narrow one), verify clean, and tighten the remediation role itself.
successCriteria: You identified every security group exposing an admin or data port to the internet and told legitimate public rules apart from findings
You revoked each world-open rule and replaced it with the narrowest source the standard allows
You verified the account with a compliance check and scoped the remediation role to describe and security group ingress changes only
hints: An external scan tells you which ports are reachable, not why. Use describe-security-groups with the ip-permission.cidr filter to find which groups allow them.
Not every 0.0.0.0/0 rule is a finding: read change-standard.txt to see which ports may be public and which sources are acceptable for admin and data ports.

Revoke first: aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id --protocol tcp --port

--cidr 0.0.0.0/0. Then add the narrow rule with authorize-security-group-ingress, using --cidr for the VPN range or --source-group for the app tier.

range.scenario: An external attack-surface scan of account 111122223333 found several open ports on public addresses, and the network team has been asked to close the gaps without breaking anything. You are on the NetOps team with the `NetOpsRemediationRole`. Map the scan's findings to security groups, decide which exposures are legitimate and which are findings, remediate each finding to least privilege following the change standard, and prove with the compliance check that the account is clean. Everything is simulated; use the terminal like the AWS CLI.

artifacts.name: change-standard.txt
artifacts.content:
Network change standard (NetOps, v2)

1. Admin ports (22/SSH, 3389/RDP) may be reachable only from the corporate VPN range 192.0.2.0/24.
2. Database and cache ports (3306/MySQL, 5432/PostgreSQL, 6379/Redis) may be reachable only from the app tier: security group sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60f06, or the app subnets (10.0.0.0/16 and narrower).
3. 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 are acceptable only for tcp/80 and tcp/443 on the public load balancer group (web-alb).
4. Remove the world-open rule first, then add the narrow rule. Do not delete security groups that are attached to instances.
5. Verify with the compliance rule no-world-open-admin-ports after every change batch.
artifacts.note: The rules your remediation must follow.

tasks.prompt: Per change-standard.txt, which of these open-to-the-internet rules is legitimate and should be kept?
options: tcp/443 on the public application load balancer group (web-alb)
tcp/22 on the admin jump host group
tcp/3306 on the orders database group
tcp/6379 on the session cache group
tasks.explanation: A public load balancer exists to receive web traffic from the internet, so tcp/80 and tcp/443 on it are expected. Administration and data stores should never be directly reachable from the internet: reaching them should require the VPN or the application tier. The audit is about separating deliberate exposure from accidental exposure.

tasks.prompt: List the world-open rules with the ip-permission.cidr filter. How many security groups expose an admin or data port to 0.0.0.0/0 (do not count the load balancer group)? Reply with a number.
tasks.explanation: Four groups expose SSH, RDP, MySQL and Redis to the internet. An external scan shows ports; mapping them to the exact group, rule and owner is what lets you fix them without guesswork. Automate this listing so that it runs regularly rather than only after a scan.

tasks.prompt: Which security group (name or id) exposes tcp/3389, remote desktop, to the internet?
tasks.explanation: RDP open to the world is a long-standing target of brute-force and credential-stuffing attempts. Admin protocols belong behind a VPN or a managed session service, with the source limited to the corporate range. Note the group is attached to a running instance, which is why you edit its rules instead of deleting it.

tasks.prompt: Remediate all four findings: revoke each 0.0.0.0/0 rule, then add the narrowest access the change standard allows (VPN range for admin ports, app tier for data ports). Run the compliance rule and paste the change attestation flag.
tasks.explanation: Least-privilege remediation has two parts: remove the exposure, then restore the access that is actually needed from the smallest possible source. Revoking alone can cause an outage, and adding a broad replacement leaves the exposure. Verifying with a compliance rule gives you evidence that the fix landed.

tasks.prompt: What is the best replacement source for the database rule on tcp/3306?
options: The app tier security group as the source, so only instances in that group can connect
0.0.0.0/0 with a strong database password
10.0.0.0/8, which covers every private address
Move the database to a non-default port and keep 0.0.0.0/0
tasks.explanation: Referencing the app tier's security group as the source follows instances as they scale and change IP, and nothing else can connect. A strong password does not make an exposed service safe, a very wide private range lets every workload in the network reach the database, and changing the port is obscurity, not access control.

tasks.prompt: Which statement about auditing and cleaning up world-open rules is correct?
options: 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 are separate rules: IPv6 exposure has to be audited and revoked in addition to the IPv4 rule
Revoking the IPv4 rule automatically removes the IPv6 rule for the same port
Deleting a security group that is attached to running instances is the fastest safe way to remove its rules
Rules open to the internet only matter if the instance has a public IP address
tasks.explanation: A security group can hold an IPv4 rule (0.0.0.0/0) and an IPv6 rule (::/0) for the same port; each must be handled separately, or you leave an open door behind. Deleting an attached group is not possible, and even for a group that could be deleted, removing the rule is the safe path. Whether an instance has a public address affects reachability, but you should still fix world-open rules because addresses change.

tasks.prompt: Tighten NetOpsRemediationRole. It must be able to describe EC2 resources and add or revoke security group ingress rules on security groups in us-east-1, and nothing else: no deleting security groups, no terminating instances, no changes in other regions.

tests.name: Can revoke ingress on a us-east-1 group
Can add ingress on a us-east-1 group
Cannot change groups in another region

tasks.explanation: A remediation role is a powerful tool: it can open ports as easily as it closes them, so scope it to the actions and resources the job needs. Describe calls are read-only and need a wildcard resource, while the ingress changes are limited to security group ARNs in one region. Pair this with CloudTrail alerts on ingress changes that add 0.0.0.0/0.

takeaways: Map scan findings to concrete security group rules, separate legitimate public exposure (a load balancer on 80/443) from accidental exposure (admin and data ports), and fix the latter.
Remediate in two steps: revoke the world-open rule, then add the narrowest source that preserves legitimate access (VPN range for admin, app-tier security group for data). Remember IPv6 (::/0).
Verify with a compliance rule, and scope the remediation role itself so the tool that closes ports cannot open them everywhere.
